Well, that "How we identify UK sites" should be "How we define a UK site".

crtasm · Nov 7, 2026

There's three other signifiers listed besides being hosted in the UK - do any of those apply to your site?

glum64 · Nov 7, 2026

I think that to identify something one should define it first. That article fails to make a difference.

zarzavat · Nov 7, 2026

What's the difference? If the UK wants to archive your website it can do so, it's public.

jMyles · Nov 7, 2026

Of course that's true.

But it's still bizarre for a legacy entity like a nation state to presume that it can identify an internet phenomenon without first explaining what it even means when declaring its intention to do so.

ghaff · Nov 7, 2026

However, it may be and in most cases is probably still copyrighted (with some exceptions such as US government content). Archiving is probably OK in most cases. Making that archive available to the public (e.g. Wayback Machine) is something that gets a blind eye turned on but there's probably not much legal backing for that--and which, to date, pretty much no one has wanted to try to build a legal case around.

jMyles · Nov 7, 2026

What you've identified is the looming great conflict of the coming decades. Legacy states presume that the internet regards reality on their terms.

If states want to legislate internet objects, they first need to very clearly explain how they define the objects which they regard as being within their purview.
